questions.question: Why can DPO train directly on a preference pair without fitting a separate reward model?
options: The KL-regularized RLHF optimum expresses reward as a beta-scaled policy/reference log-ratio, which can be inserted into the Bradley–Terry loss
DPO discards the preference signal and copies the reference model
Pairwise preferences contain no information about rewards
DPO replaces the policy with a fixed classifier
questions.explanation: The closed-form KL-RL optimum gives r(x,y) = beta log(pi(y|x)/pi_ref(y|x)) plus a prompt constant. Substituting that difference into the preference likelihood yields the DPO objective.

questions.question: In the toy code, what distinguishes IPO's update from DPO's update?
options: IPO uses no preference pairs at all
IPO drives the log-ratio difference toward a finite target 1/(2 beta) instead of the DPO sigmoid margin alone
IPO removes the policy and trains only the reference
IPO ranks actions by token count rather than preference
questions.explanation: train_dpo sets target = 1/(2*beta) for variant="ipo" and penalizes the squared deviation from that target. This bounds the implicit reward gap that a tiny DPO preference probability could otherwise inflate.

questions.question: When is KTO the appropriate member of this family for the data shape?
options: When every example has a paired winner and loser of equal length
When a reference-free loss is mandatory and no labels exist
When examples carry unpaired desirable/undesirable labels and loss aversion should weight undesirable outcomes
When the only available signal is a model's tokenizer
questions.explanation: train_kto consumes (action, desirable) labels rather than (winner, loser) pairs. Its undesirable branch uses a larger loss-aversion factor, matching KTO's prospect-theoretic motivation.

questions.question: What is SimPO's defining structural change relative to DPO?
options: It adds a second reference policy and removes the margin
It uses only negative labels and no chosen response
It keeps DPO's reference log-ratio but changes the target to a scalar reward head
It removes the reference policy and uses length-normalized policy log-probabilities with a margin
questions.explanation: train_simpo computes beta*(log pi_w/length - log pi_l/length) - gamma directly from the policy. The demo's one-action lengths are all 1, but the length normalization is the intended production distinction.

questions.question: What does the BPO branch add to the DPO gradient in this repository?
options: An anchor penalty that pushes the chosen log-probability toward or above the reference value
A tokenizer reinitialization after every pair
A reward-model ensemble over six policies
A rule that always lowers the chosen response probability
questions.explanation: The BPO code computes anchor_pen = -(log_pi_w - log_ref_w) and adds a term involving grad_logprob(w). That directly counters degraded chosen responses instead of allowing the chosen log-prob to fall while the rejected one falls faster.

questions.question: What do the DPO-family scaling results imply about using a direct alignment loss?
options: Removing an explicit RM removes all Goodhart pressure
Direct alignment algorithms can still over-optimize, so held-out gold or capability evaluation remains necessary
Only IPO can over-optimize; DPO, SimPO, and KTO cannot
A sufficiently large paired dataset makes the gold reward monotonic by theorem
questions.explanation: The optimization target is still a proxy derived from preferences. The lesson's scaling result preserves the peak-and-collapse pattern, so a DPO run needs a held-out target rather than only its training loss or win rate.
